tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: Mozart wrote twelve variations on this French children’s song, “Ah, vous dirai-je, maman.” It is the same tune as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.”

songs.title: Minuet in G
songs.composer: J. S. Bach (attributed; Christian Petzold), BWV Anh. 114, left hand simplified
songs.source: J. S. Bach (attributed; Christian Petzold), BWV Anh. 114, left hand simplified

tips.label: Key signature:
tips.text: The sharp on the F line means every F is played as F♯, the black key just below G.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: This minuet is in the notebook Bach kept for his wife, Anna Magdalena. Scholars now think Christian Petzold wrote it, but Bach’s family played it at home.

songs.title: Eine kleine Nachtmusik (opening)
songs.composer: W. A. Mozart (1756–1791), K. 525, first movement
songs.source: W. A. Mozart (1756–1791), K. 525, first movement

tips.label: Both hands play the same notes
tips.text: an octave apart, just as the whole orchestra plays this opening together. Mozart wrote it in 1787.

songs.title: Amazing Grace
songs.composer: Words: John Newton (1779); tune: NEW BRITAIN (American, 1829)
songs.source: Words: John Newton (1779); tune: NEW BRITAIN (American, 1829)

tips.label: Pickup note:
tips.text: the song starts on beat 3, so the first bar has only one note, “A-”.

songs.title: Doxology (Old Hundredth)
songs.composer: Words: Thomas Ken (1674); tune: OLD 100TH, Genevan Psalter (1551)
songs.source: Words: Thomas Ken (1674); tune: OLD 100TH, Genevan Psalter (1551)

songs.title: Jesus Loves Me
songs.composer: Words: Anna B. Warner (1860); music: William B. Bradbury (1862)
songs.source: Words: Anna B. Warner (1860); music: William B. Bradbury (1862)

tips.label: Dotted rhythm:
tips.text: a dotted quarter plus an eighth sounds “long-short”, like a skip.

songs.title: Go Tell Aunt Rhody
songs.composer: American folk song (tune from J.-J. Rousseau, 1752)
songs.source: American folk song (tune from J.-J. Rousseau, 1752)

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: This tune came from a French opera written in 1752. American families sang it for generations, and it is a favorite first song for fiddlers.

tips.label: Hand position:
tips.text: Thumb on C, then 2 on D, 3 on E, 4 on G and 5 on A. The fourth finger skips over F.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: Stephen Foster wrote this in 1850. Fiddle and banjo players have kept it going ever since.

songs.title: When the Saints Go Marching In

tips.label: Rest first:
tips.text: Most lines start with a quarter rest. Count “1” silently, then play on 2.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: This spiritual is a favorite at bluegrass jams, gospel sings and New Orleans parades.

songs.title: Cripple Creek
songs.source: Traditional; A part after Bill Hensley's 1940 playing, moved to G

tips.label: Hand position:
tips.text: Thumb on D, 2 on E, 3 on G, 4 on A, 5 on B. No F in this tune, so finger 3 skips it.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: “Goin’ up Cripple Creek” is often the very first tune banjo players learn.

songs.title: Old Joe Clark
songs.source: Traditional; A part, moved from A to G

tips.label: The mountain sound:
tips.text: This tune is in G but uses F, not F♯. That lowered note gives old fiddle tunes their lonesome, mountain sound.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: Fiddlers in the Kentucky and North Carolina mountains have played Old Joe Clark for well over a hundred years.

songs.title: Soldier’s Joy
songs.source: Traditional; A part after Fiddlin' John Carson

tips.label: Key of D:
tips.text: Two sharps: every F is F♯ and every C is C♯. Fiddlers love D because it rings on the open strings.

tips.label: Did you know?
tips.text: Soldier’s Joy is one of the oldest tunes still played at American jams. It came over from Scotland in the 1700s.

courses.title: Piano Foundations 1
courses.blurb: Posture, finding notes, reading the staff, and both hands together, with a Mozart theme.

cards.p: Sit on the front half of the bench, feet flat, with your elbows a little in front of your body and level with the keys.
Let your hand hang loose at your side, then bring it to the keys keeping that natural curve, as if holding a ball. Play on the fingertips.
Thumbs are 1, pointers 2, middles 3, rings 4 and pinkies 5, on both hands. The small numbers above notes tell you which finger to use.
C is the white key just left of each group of two black keys. Middle C is the one nearest the center of your piano.
A filled note with a stem is a quarter note: one beat. A hollow note with a stem is a half note: two beats.
This piece has 2 beats in every bar (the 2/4 at the start). Count “1, 2” in every bar while you play.
When notes move from a line to the next space (or space to line), you move to the very next white key. That is a step.
Before you play, look at the shape: is the tune going up, down, or repeating? In bars 9–16 it walks down by steps.
The lower staff has the bass clef. Its two dots sit around the F line, which is the F below Middle C.
Put L.H. finger 5 on the C an octave below Middle C. Here the left hand plays one long note in each bar.
Look straight down the music: notes stacked above each other are played at the same moment.
Practice mode waits for you, so take your time. Then try it with the beat. Speed comes later.
You now know every part of this theme. Play it from start to finish with both hands.
In “Play with the beat”, switch on Band for a bass and chords to play along with you.

courses.title: Bach & Mozart 1
courses.blurb: Key signatures, eighth notes and phrasing through Bach’s Minuet in G and Mozart’s Night Music.

cards.p: The sharp at the start of every line is the key signature. It means every F in the piece is F♯, the black key just left of G.
R.H. thumb on G above Middle C. The tune leaps from D down to G and climbs back up.
Eighth notes have a flag or a beam. Two of them fit in one beat. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and”.
The curved slurs mean legato: connect the notes smoothly, one finger lifting as the next goes down.
The left hand plays mostly long dotted half notes (3 beats). In bars 7–8 it gets busier. Read carefully.
A dot above or below a note means staccato: short and light, bouncing off the key.
The last two bars bring the music home to G. That “coming home” is called a cadence. Let the final G ring.
Both hands play the same note names, 8 white keys apart. That distance is an octave.
The little rests between notes make Mozart’s opening crisp. Lift your hands exactly on time.

courses.title: Hymns 1
courses.blurb: Pickup notes, 3/4 time and steady hymn playing with Amazing Grace, the Doxology and Jesus Loves Me.

cards.p: In 3/4 each bar has three beats. A dotted half note fills the whole bar.
Amazing Grace starts on beat 3: count “1, 2,” then play “A-” on 3.
Let the right hand sing a little louder than the left. The left hand plays one bass note per bar.
This tune is over 450 years old. Each line starts with a long note, moves in steady quarters, and rests at the end.
The rests at the end of each line are like a choir taking a breath. Lift both hands together.
Each line of words takes two bars. The tune repeats a lot. Spot the patterns before you play.
The dotted half on “me” lasts three beats. Count it out so you don’t rush.

courses.title: Folk Songs 1
courses.blurb: Dotted rhythms and toe-tapping tunes with Stephen Foster’s Oh! Susanna. Then on to Old-Time & Traditional 1.

cards.p: A dot adds half the note’s value. A dotted quarter lasts 1½ beats, then a quick eighth finishes the beat: “long-short”.
The left hand plays steady half notes like a bass. Switch on Band in Play mode for the full pickin’ sound.

courses.title: Old-Time & Traditional 1
courses.blurb: Front-porch songs with a bluegrass bass: Go Tell Aunt Rhody, Camptown Races and When the Saints.

cards.p: Long before bluegrass had a name, families in the mountains played simple tunes like this on fiddle and banjo. Bluegrass grew out of these songs.
R.H. thumb on Middle C, one finger per key up to G. Every note in this song is under your hand, so keep your eyes on the music.
A bluegrass bass player bounces between two notes: the chord’s name note (the root), then the note five steps lower (the fifth). For a C chord that’s C, then G.
For G7 the left hand plays G, then D. L.H. 5 on the low G, thumb on D, and finger 2 on C.
The left hand plays a half note on beat 1 and another on beat 3. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” and land both hands together on 1 and 3.
This tune uses C D E G A. Put fingers 1-2-3 on C D E, then 4 on G and 5 on A. Finger 4 skips over F.
E up to G skips a white key. On the staff that’s a line to the next line (or space to space).
Bluegrass never stops for mistakes. In “Play with the beat”, keep going even if a note slips. Turn on Band for the full sound.

lessons.title: When the Saints: rests & long notes

cards.p: A quarter rest fills beat 1. Count “1” silently, then play “Oh when the” on beats 2, 3 and 4.
A hollow note with no stem is a whole note: hold it for all four beats while the left hand keeps bouncing.

lessons.title: When the Saints, the whole song

cards.p: In bar 12 the left hand moves down to F, then C. Find the low F before you start.
Play it with Band on. When it feels easy, raise the speed a little each day.

courses.title: Bluegrass 1
courses.blurb: Real fiddle tunes from jam sessions: Cripple Creek, Old Joe Clark and Soldier’s Joy. Eighth-note runs and the mountain sound.

cards.p: Bluegrass players learn tunes like this by ear at jams. The melody runs in quick eighth notes, two to a beat.
The first bar is only two eighth notes on the “and” of beat 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4 and” and come in on the last half of 4.
This tune is in G, so the left hand bounces G, then D (L.H. 5 on G, thumb on D). In bars 3 and 5 the chord changes halfway.

lessons.title: Old Joe Clark: the mountain sound

cards.p: Old Joe Clark is in G but uses plain F. That one note makes it sound old and lonesome. Musicians call this sound Mixolydian.
R.H. thumb on the C above Middle C. In bar 2 the hand hops down for B and the low G, then comes back.

lessons.title: Old Joe Clark, the whole A part

cards.p: G chord: G then D. F chord: F then C. The F chord matches the plain F in the tune.
Before each hop, glance at the next bar so your hand is already on its way.
The key signature has F♯ and C♯. Every F and C in the piece is played on the black key just to the right.
Thumb on D, 3 on F♯, 5 on A. In bar 2 the hand moves up so 2 is on A and 5 reaches high D.
D chord: D then the A below it. A chord: A then E. Keep it steady even when the right hand gets busy.
Turn on Band in “Play with the beat”. Add 5 to the speed each day until it feels like a real jam.
